text: Escalation isn't throwing an alert over a wall and moving on -- it's a handoff, and a clean one lets Tier 2 start exactly where Tier 1 left off instead of redoing work that's already done. Everything this chapter has covered so far, triage, validation, scoping, and the case note, exists to produce exactly the pieces that handoff needs.

A clean handoff gives Tier 2 four things: the classification Tier 1 already reached, with the reasoning behind it; the scope already established, including what hasn't been checked yet; the evidence already gathered in the case note; and a clear reason for escalating -- which of the three criteria from Lesson 18 applied here.

Skipping any of those pieces doesn't save time, it just moves the missing work downstream onto a team with less availability. A Tier 2 analyst who gets "this looks bad, escalating" with no case note has to re-validate from scratch -- slower overall than if Tier 1 had simply finished the job themselves.

Escalations travel through a few real channels. A ticketing system is the default -- the case note and evidence get attached and routed to the Tier 2 queue, worked in order. A direct handoff, a call, page, or channel message, supplements the ticket for anything that can't wait, like active exfiltration. Severity-based routing decides which path a case takes: a confirmed critical incident gets an immediate page on top of the ticket, while a high-but-not-urgent case rides the normal queue.

Put together on the file-share example from Lesson 18: Tier 1 validates, scopes, documents, files a ticket with the case note attached, and sends a direct message because the severity calls for it. Tier 2 opens the case already knowing what happened. That closes out Chapter 5 -- next, Chapter 6 turns to building a SOC dashboard that analysts actually use to track a whole queue of cases like this one.
